body.text: India’s free trade agreement (FTA) strategy is entering a different phase. For much of the past decade, success was measured by how many markets New Delhi could bring within its preferential trade network. As that network expands, the more important question is becoming whether Indian firms can actually use the access being negotiated on their behalf.
Taken together, these numbers suggest that India’s trade strategy is shifting from selective agreements to building a broad preferential trade network.

Union Minister of Commerce and Industry Piyush Goyal’s announcement in Tokyo regarding FTAs (on August 24) points to the scale of the shift. India has signed nine FTAs in four years, with another eight or nine groupings at various stages of negotiations. The government has set an ambitious target of bringing around 75 per cent of global trade within the country’s preferential trade network. This marks a significant expansion in the scope and pace of India’s trade diplomacy.
But coverage is only the first part of the equation. The more consequential question for India’s exporters is what happens after an agreement is signed.

One number that receives considerably less attention is FTA utilisation. According to the Global Trade Research Initiative, India currently has 15 implemented FTAs, with roughly nine more either awaiting implementation or under negotiation. Yet, only 20-30 per cent of eligible Indian exports reportedly use preferential tariffs under existing agreements. In contrast, utilisation by exporters from partner countries into India is estimated at 60-70 per cent. The Economist Intelligence Unit has similarly placed India’s historical utilisation rate at roughly a quarter, compared with 70-80 per cent among developed economies.

The precise figure varies by methodology, agreement, and sector. The broader pattern, however, is difficult to ignore: Indian exporters do not appear to be using preferential market access to the same extent as exporters from several partner economies.

This matters because an FTA does not generate an export benefit merely by lowering a tariff on paper. A firm has to know that the preference exists, establish that its product qualifies, satisfy rules of origin, obtain the necessary documentation, and absorb the administrative cost of claiming the benefit.

GTRI’s own analysis suggests that this is precisely why smaller firms often opt out: where most favoured nation (MFN) tariffs abroad are already low, the compliance cost of certification and paperwork can exceed the tariff saved. For a large corporation with dedicated compliance teams, these costs are manageable. For a smaller manufacturer or trading firm, they can change the calculation altogether.

The result is a paradox worth pondering over: India can negotiate progressively wider access to overseas markets while a significant share of its own exporters continues to trade under the standard tariff regime rather than the preferential one negotiated on their behalf.

This does not diminish the strategic rationale for expanding India’s network of trade agreements. Diversification has become increasingly important as supply chains adjust to geopolitical uncertainty, as China-plus-one strategies evolve, and as major economies reassess their trade relationships.

Greater access to Europe, the Gulf, East Asia, and other markets can reduce concentration risks and give Indian producers more opportunities to integrate into global value chains. But diversification of markets and utilisation of preferences are different objectives. The first is largely a question of diplomacy and negotiation for better opportunities. The second is a question of domestic competitiveness, information, compliance, and institutional capacity, and that is where the record is weaker.
When tariffs work differently

Another complication becomes more important as India’s FTA network expands: the starting point is not always symmetrical. India’s trade-weighted MFN tariff stands at approximately 12.6 per cent, with individual rates ranging as high as 150 per cent on sensitive lines. Several economies with which India has preferential arrangements, such as Singapore, Japan, Australia, Malaysia, and the UAE, already run average MFN tariffs close to zero or in the low single digits. The commercial effect follows directly from this gap.

The asymmetry matters because preferential access does not create equal commercial gains on both sides. When India grants preferential access, foreign producers gain a meaningful price advantage in the Indian market because they move from a relatively high baseline tariff to zero. When Indian exporters receive preferential access in a partner market that already has low tariffs, the incremental benefit is naturally smaller, since there was lower tariff to begin with.

This does not make the agreements inherently unequal or undesirable; market access involves far more than tariff rates, and value can differ substantially across sectors, but it does mean that headline concessions on both sides are not always commercially equivalent.
The issue becomes more complicated when the tariff structure on inputs is considered.

As finished products increasingly enter India at preferential or zero duties from the ASEAN region, Japan, South Korea, Australia, and the UAE, Indian manufacturers can still face relatively high duties on raw materials and intermediate goods sourced from countries outside the FTA network, among them China. This can create an inverted incentive, where an overseas producer brings a finished product into India at a lower effective tariff than what an Indian manufacturer pays to source the inputs needed to make a competing product.

The resulting pressure should not be attributed to FTAs alone. Trade deficits reflect many factors, including domestic demand, industrial competitiveness, exchange rates, energy imports, and the structure of supply chains.

But the trend lines are notable: India’s trade deficit with ASEAN rose by roughly 381 per cent between 2007-09 and 2023-25, with the deficits against Japan and South Korea rising by a comparable order of magnitude over the same period. This does not, by itself, establish that the agreements produced a negative outcome. But it does raise a fair policy question: whether India’s domestic tariff structure on industrial inputs is being reviewed and adjusted at a pace that keeps up with the expansion of its preferential trade network.
Making market access work

The answer need not be fewer FTAs. It may instead be closer integration between trade negotiations and the domestic policies needed to use them. The India-EU agreement illustrates both the opportunity and the stakes. Concluded in January and expected to be formally signed by December, with implementation likely by February-March 2027, the deal covers a bloc that accounts for roughly a quarter of global GDP and about a third of global trade.

It is expected to offer near-zero-duty access to close to 93 per cent of Indian exports to the EU market, access that will be substantial by any measure once it takes effect. But the scale of the opportunity will ultimately depend on how many Indian firms are equipped to use it. A tariff concession that exists in an agreement but goes unused by exporters has limited economic value, whatever its size on paper.

This suggests that India’s FTA dashboard needs another column. Alongside the number of agreements, countries covered, and share of global trade, it would be useful for policymakers to track and publish utilisation rates by agreement, sector, and firm size.

Such data could clarify where the gap actually lies, whether exporters lack information about the preferences available to them, whether rules of origin are too cumbersome relative to the savings on offer, or whether Indian firms face deeper competitiveness constraints that a tariff preference alone cannot offset.

A more targeted policy response could follow from that data: simplified rules-of-origin certification where feasible, sector-specific outreach to help MSME exporters understand and claim preferences, more predictable customs procedures, and a periodic review of tariffs on industrial inputs so the gap with finished-goods concessions does not keep widening with every new agreement signed.

This would also change how FTA success gets discussed. The number of agreements and the share of global trade covered are genuine indicators of India’s growing integration with the international economy, but they are not, on their own, substitutes for export performance.

India’s trade diplomacy has moved decisively towards building a wider network of preferential markets over the last four years. The next phase of that effort lies in making the network commercially usable for the firms it was built for. The missing variable in India’s FTA arithmetic is not another agreement; it is utilisation, and that is the number worth watching as closely as the headline count.
Tarun Agarwal is a Policy Research Fellow, Indian Association of International Studies (IAIS), New Delhi. where he leads the International Relations and Conflict vertical.
